title: The Listening Winter
premise: Urban explorer Xanthe Joubert descends into unmapped tunnels beneath the dying village of Hollowmere and finds a second church below the first—one whose bell still rings, though its twin above was melted down in 1911. The villagers have kept a bargain for a century: each harvest, something is invited in, and in exchange the village survives winters that should have killed everyone. When Xanthe's intrusion breaks the old invitation's seal, the entity turns its attention to them, and the village elders decide a stranger is a far cheaper offering than one of their own children. Xanthe, a lifelong nonbeliever, must survive until sunrise and choose between exposing the truth—which would doom Hollowmere's children to the listening dark—and accepting an inheritance they never wanted, becoming the next keeper of the bell. In the end, Xanthe rings the bell themselves, binding the entity to a new bargain and inheriting the village's terrible covenant.
about_author: Rafael Ishikawa is the pen name of a former surveyor who spent a decade mapping decommissioned infrastructure across rural Europe before turning to fiction. They write horror rooted in the uncanny geography of forgotten places, and The Listening Winter is their third novel.

chapters.title: The Survey That Isn't
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Arriving in Hollowmere to map a storm-drain anomaly, Xanthe notes the village's too-clean streets, the salt lines at every doorway, and the church tower's empty bell frame. The emotional beat is confident skepticism; Xanthe treats the villagers' cold stares as small-town xenophobia, not warning.

chapters.title: Salt at the Threshold
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. A shopkeeper, Maren Ostrow, refuses to sell rope to Xanthe and quietly slips a paper packet of salt into their pack instead. An old man on the green tells them to be indoors by dusk on Friday. The beat is unease: kindness and menace arriving in the same gesture.

chapters.title: Below the First Church
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, descending. The drain opens into a vaulted undercroft older than any record, and beneath it a second nave, complete, intact, its altar black with centuries of tallow. The beat is the thrill of discovery curdling into wrongness as Xanthe realizes the tunnel wasn't abandoned—it was maintained.

chapters.title: The Bell That Was Melted
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. In the lower nave hangs a bronze bell, and parish records Xanthe photographed earlier prove its twin was melted for war metal in 1911. As they touch it, the bell tolls once, though nothing moves. The beat is vertigo: the first hard crack in Xanthe's unbelief.

chapters.title: What the Elders Keep
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. The village council convenes in the upper church; Maren argues the stranger must be told the terms, while elder Corvin Hale insists the intruder is simply this year's answer to the debt. The beat is dread and moral compromise—readers see the machinery of the bargain turning.

chapters.title: Nineteen Eleven
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, reading a hidden parish ledger in the undercroft. The entries record a century of 'invitations'—names, dates, and harvest moons—and stop abruptly at Xanthe's arrival, the ink already waiting. The beat is horror of implication: the book expected them.

chapters.title: The Harvest Moon Rises Early
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Trapped in the tunnels by a rockfall that shouldn't have been possible, Xanthe hears the lower bell ringing continuously now, and something below answering it in kind. The beat is claustrophobic panic as night falls early and the moon rises fat and red.

chapters.title: Invited In
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The entity arrives—not a shape but a listening presence that fills the nave and repeats back every thought Xanthe has ever tried not to think. The beat is psychological violation: unbelief becomes impossible when the unbelief itself is spoken back to them.

chapters.title: Terms of the House
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren descends against the council's orders to find Xanthe alive, and explains the covenant: the entity is fed an invitation each harvest, and the village endures. She reveals the rockfall was Hale's doing. The beat is reluctant alliance between liar and liar.

chapters.title: The Children's Ledger
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, in the village archive with Maren. They discover the early invitations were children, given willingly by desperate parents in the famine winter of 1911, and that the entity's hunger has only ever grown. The beat is grief and rising anger at the inherited sin.

chapters.title: Hale's Bargain
chapters.summary: Corvin Hale's POV. Hale, whose own daughter comes of age this harvest, justifies offering the stranger instead; his chapter reveals the corruption at the covenant's heart—each keeper has bent the terms to spare their own. The beat is chilling self-justification.

chapters.title: Sunrise Deadline
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Maren explains the one rule that matters: what is invited in must be answered before sunrise or it takes what it wants. Xanthe, injured and half-frozen, begins the climb out with the ledger as leverage. The beat is grim resolve.

chapters.title: The Village That Watches
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, emerging at dawn to find every villager standing in the street, silent, waiting to see what came up out of the ground. Hale demands the ledger; Maren stands between them. The beat is open confrontation—the village's mask finally off.

chapters.title: Offered
chapters.summary: Hale's POV. The council votes to seal Xanthe back below as this year's invitation, and Hale's daughter Ilsa, learning what her father has arranged, quietly unlocks the cellar where Xanthe is held. The beat is the corruption theme inverted: the next generation refuses the inheritance.

chapters.title: Flight Through the Salt Lines
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Xanthe and Ilsa flee through fields where the salt has been scattered, and the entity follows—not through the tunnels now, but along the land itself, arriving wherever the salt is broken. The beat is desperate, breathless pursuit.

chapters.title: What It Wants
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, cornered at the ruined mill. The entity speaks plainly for the first time: it doesn't want a body, it wants a keeper—someone to ring the bell and hold the invitation, or it will take everything. The beat is terrible clarity about the true price of survival.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Chair
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren confesses she was meant to be the keeper thirty years ago and fled, and that the village's slow decay since—dead fields, dead bell, dead children—is her unpaid debt. The beat is confession as reckoning.

chapters.title: Council of Knives
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Xanthe returns to the village and presents the ledger to the assembled families, exposing a century of traded children and Hale's tampering. The villagers fracture; Hale moves to seize the ledger by force. The beat is the village devouring itself.

chapters.title: The Bell Above, The Bell Below
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, as the harvest moon peaks. Realizing the two bells are one instrument split in 1911, Xanthe descends alone to the lower nave, understanding that only a willing keeper can ring it. The beat is sacrificial decision—the skeptic choosing to believe with their hands.

chapters.title: Invitation Answered
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, climax. As the entity closes in, Xanthe rings the lower bell; above, the empty tower hums in resonance, and the covenant re-forges around Xanthe's name in the ledger. The entity withdraws, bound. The beat is awe and cost intertwined.

chapters.title: The Inheritance
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, aftermath. Sunrise comes; Hale is gone into the tunnels, whether fled or taken no one will say. Maren and Ilsa bury the ledger's children's names properly, and the village, for the first time in a century, plants spring wheat. The beat is exhausted, imperfect grace.

chapters.title: The Listening Winter
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, epilogue. Xanthe stays as keeper, living in the shadow of the tower, and on the first night of winter hears the bell toll softly once—acknowledgment, or appetite. They salt their own doorway and leave a page blank in the ledger. The beat is quiet, unresolved dread: the price of survival is never paid once.
